title: The Real GPA Was the Friends We Made Along the Way
author: Kevin Stinehart
summary: Third-grade teacher Kevin Stinehart argues that AI forces schools to ask what an assignment was meant to change in the learner, since a machine can now supply the product without the experience. He contrasts using AI to make assessment graphs, which saved him time for the thinking that mattered, with using it to paint or complete work a child needs to practice. He cites learning-versus-performance research and a 2025 randomized trial in which students using GPT tools did better during assisted practice but about 17 percent worse without assistance. Using his daughter's state-champion band as an analogy, he says the trophy is not the point; the rehearsal, friendships and character formed along the way are. He then shows a forest map-making lesson designed around the nine areas of his Architecture of Childhood framework, and proposes evaluating the opportunities schools provide rather than only final performance.
points: The key question about AI is not whether it can complete an assignment but whether completing it was supposed to change what the learner can do.
Removing a barrier can open up learning, but removing the very activity a child needs to practice bypasses it.
Polished output during assisted practice is a poor guide to retention, as shown by the study where AI users scored about 17 percent lower unassisted.
A real-audience project, such as maps for kindergarteners, can embed self-regulation, agency, resilience and responsibility in academic content.
Schools should examine the opportunities children get each day to decide, revise and contribute, not just their end performance.
quotes: The question isn’t whether a machine can complete an assignment. It’s whether completing the assignment was supposed to change what the person could understand and do.
Removing a barrier can open up learning. Removing the very activity a child needs to practice can bypass it completely.
Students with the AI tools scored better during assisted practice but scored about 17 percent lower without assistance later on.
A completed worksheet may show understanding, or it may show that a child found a way to fill every blank. As a teacher, I need to know the difference.
Press a button, collect the ring, go to the statehouse. The trophy would be identical. The kids receiving it would not.

A transcript is useful, but it’s also a very small document to ask to hold a whole person. Quarterly report cards, GPAs, academic awards, and standardized test scores can’t hold a candle to the social skills, characteristics, life lessons, creativity, work ethic, and people skills a child needs to be capable, resilient, and ready for the next stage in life.
We spend enormous energy measuring their end performance. I want us to examine the opportunities we provide each day with the same seriousness.
In a lesson, we can ask who does the thinking. Across a school day, we can ask where children have room to move, play, make choices, communicate, and contribute.
